RagShortTexts: Walrus ivory reaches distant buyers through successive exchanges.
Hunting, carriage and intermediaries affect its price.

Variants.Content: Northern ivory and furs pass through hunters, buyers and carriers. Value must cover hunting, carriage and storage losses. A high final price need not reach the hunter, who may not know the eventual use.
Ivory escorts guard against breakage and missing parcels. Handover records of pieces and damage prevent blame for a crack that predates their journey.
Taxing distant goods requires owners and values. Excess demands divert trade; market prices without carriage costs exaggerate taxable returns.
Hunters need food and tools before the next buyer arrives. Traders inspect ivory and damage; rarity alone does not supply a paying customer.
